summaries.gardner: Palo Alto Networks fits several Rule Breaker traits: it leads a fast-growing industry (28.4% network-security share in 2024 per Omdia), has strong price momentum (about +86% over the past year) and is widely called overvalued. It is weaker on consumer brand recognition and on being a founder-led, top-dog-and-first-mover in a brand-new market, since firewalls are a mature category it is extending into AI, identity and cloud.
summaries.buffett: The business has a real moat through switching costs and $21.2B of remaining performance obligations, and it generates strong free cash flow ($4,113M in FY2026). But GAAP returns on capital are low after the ~$25B CyberArk deal, share count has risen from 709M to 817M diluted, and at roughly $325B market cap there is no margin of safety, so it is a poor fit for Buffett's price discipline.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the lock-in of security infrastructure and the quality of the franchise, but would dislike heavy stock-based pay, an acquisition-driven strategy and a valuation near 990 times trailing GAAP earnings. It looks like a wonderful business at a price that leaves little room for error.
summaries.lynch: It fits Lynch's 'fast grower' category, with revenue up 24.5% in FY2026 and guided 23-24% for FY2027, partly from acquisitions. It fails his price tests: forward P/E around 90 on non-GAAP EPS guidance of $4.16-$4.19 is far above the earnings growth rate, insiders are net sellers and it is anything but overlooked by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: It scores well on Fisher's growth points: a long sales runway, steady new products (XSIAM, Prisma AIRS, Cortex Cloud), a strong sales organisation with more than 8,700 channel partners, and management focused on long-term platform building. Weaker points are thin GAAP profit margins (6.1% operating margin in FY2026) and dilution from stock compensation and acquisitions.
summaries.graham: It fails nearly all of Graham's defensive-investor tests: it reported GAAP net losses in FY2020-FY2022, pays no dividend, and trades at about 990 times trailing GAAP earnings and roughly 12 times book value. Only its size and strong balance sheet pass.
summaries.thiel: It answers several of Thiel's questions well: a dominant position in network security, a powerful distribution engine, a world-class management team and good timing for AI-driven security. It is less of a 'zero to one' monopoly because rivals like Fortinet, CrowdStrike, Zscaler and Microsoft offer close substitutes in each of its markets.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders benefiting from AI and cloud, with efficient growth; PANW's revenue growth plus FCF margin of about 60 (24.5% + 35.8%) fits that well. The concerns would be valuation after the stock roughly doubled in 2026 and how much of the growth is acquired rather than organic.
summaries.druckenmiller: The stock has strong momentum and a clear catalyst set (CyberArk cross-sell, AI security demand, NGS ARR up 63% to $9.10B), which Druckenmiller-style trend following likes. Earnings growth, however, is not accelerating on a per-share basis (FY2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance implies about 9% growth), so the setup relies on revenue and sentiment more than earnings acceleration.
summaries.smith: It partly meets Fundsmith's 'good company' test with high gross margins (70.4%), recurring revenue and strong cash conversion, but GAAP return on capital is low and it is acquisitive. At a free-cash-flow yield near 1.3% it clearly fails 'don't overpay'.
summaries.greenblatt: It scores poorly on the Magic Formula: GAAP operating income of $695M is tiny relative to an enterprise value of roughly $319B, and return on tangible capital is diluted by $22B of goodwill and $7B of intangibles after acquisitions.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high rates. PANW has the first leg (sticky, high-margin security subscriptions) and a capable CEO, but reinvestment is mainly via expensive acquisitions with uncertain returns, and the price is very high.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach wants low-risk, high-uncertainty bargains, often in distressed businesses. PANW is a fully valued, widely owned market darling (88% institutional ownership), so it does not fit his 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup.
summaries.wood: PANW sits at the crossroads of AI and cloud security, with Prisma AIRS, AI agent security (Koi, Portkey) and AI-driven SOC (XSIAM), which aligns with ARK's interest in AI. It is still more an established incumbent than a pure disruptive innovator, and costs are not falling in the way ARK's Wright's-law thesis looks for.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry and a reasonable price. PANW is predictable and cash-generative with high barriers, but it is complex, acquisitive and far from cheap, so it only partly fits.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model requires a company to pass its scale savings back to customers. PANW's platformization offers (bundles and free transition periods) share some value, but it remains a premium-priced vendor, so it only partly fits the Nomad model.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets with painful problems and great teams; cybersecurity is a large, urgent market and PANW is the scale leader. As a mature public company rather than an early-stage disruptor, it is more of a 'big market, strong team' fit than a classic Sequoia startup.
summaries.nash: PANW passes Nash's growth, balance-sheet, secular-trend and Rule of 40 tests (24.5% growth, about 36% FCF margin, cash and investments well above $1,774M of debt). It fails his instant-kill operating-margin rule (6.1% GAAP), shows an acquisition spree and insider selling, and its valuation (forward P/E around 90, PEG far above 1) is not attractive.

momentum.evidence: The shares are up about 86% over the past year and roughly 104% year to date in 2026 (52-week range $141.67-$419.91), far ahead of the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Nikesh Arora (ex-Google, SoftBank) and founder/CTO Nir Zuk lead the company, and institutions hold about 88% of the shares.

g6.evidence: With a trailing GAAP P/E near 990 and some analysts publishing targets far below the price (e.g., a $206 valuation case after the CyberArk close), the stock is often called overvalued.

simple.evidence: The core idea, selling security software and firewalls on subscriptions, is understandable, but its many product lines (Strata, Prisma, Cortex, Idira, Chronosphere, Unit 42) and heavy non-GAAP adjustments make it complex for a generalist.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $3,408.4M in FY2020 to $11,480M in FY2026, but GAAP profits only turned consistently positive in FY2023 after losses in FY2020-FY2022.

integrity.evidence: Management reports clearly and has a long beat record, but heavy stock-based compensation, large CEO equity awards and reliance on non-GAAP metrics weaken alignment with owners.

b6.evidence: Its platformization strategy is distinctive, but large, fast acquisitions (CyberArk ~$25B, Chronosphere, Koi, Portkey, Console, Embrace) look partly like empire building.

roic.evidence: FY2026 GAAP operating income of $695M is small relative to $27,492M of equity, though it uses little debt ($1,774M of convertible notes).

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $4,113M (35.8% of revenue), far above GAAP net income of $307M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings are small ($2,791M at July 31, 2026); value creation has come mainly from reinvested cash flow and stock-funded acquisitions, which have grown revenue but also the share count.

safety.evidence: At about $325B market cap against $4,113M of FY2026 free cash flow (about 1.3% yield), the price is well above any conservative value estimate.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of roughly 90 on FY2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance of $4.16-$4.19 is expensive for ~23-24% revenue growth that includes acquired revenue.

mu5.evidence: Firewalls and security contracts are sticky, but it could be hurt by Microsoft bundling, a botched CyberArk integration or a major breach of its own products.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest heavily in R&D and acquisitions in a growing market, but returns on recent large acquisitions such as CyberArk are unproven.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear fast grower: revenue grew 24.5% in FY2026 and is guided to $14.10-$14.20B (23-24% growth) in FY2027.

ly3.evidence: Forward P/E near 90 is far above expected EPS growth of about 9% (FY2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance $4.16-$4.19 versus $3.84).

runway.evidence: New markets such as identity security, observability and AI agent security add to a cybersecurity market that keeps growing with cloud and AI adoption.

ly7.evidence: Insiders were net sellers (about $9.2M in the last 90 days, no buyers) and diluted shares rose from 709M in FY2025 to 817M in Q4 FY2026 after the CyberArk stock deal.

ly8.evidence: It is heavily covered (about 51 analysts estimate its revenue) and widely owned by institutions (about 88%).

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching new products, such as Cortex XSIAM, Cortex Cloud and Prisma AIRS, and added identity and observability lines in FY2026.

fi3.evidence: R&D and integrated acquisitions have produced fast-growing products, helping NGS ARR rise 63% to $9.10B in Q4 FY2026.

fi4.evidence: It has a large, aggressive sales force and more than 8,700 channel partners, and doubled platform customers to 2,280 in a year by Q3 FY2026.

longterm.evidence: Management accepted near-term billing pressure from platformization offers and lower GAAP margins in FY2026 to build a broader long-term platform.

gr1.evidence: It is a large company with $11,480M of FY2026 revenue and a market cap of about $325B.

ni10.evidence: It reported GAAP net losses in FY2020 (-$267.0M), FY2021 (-$498.9M) and FY2022 (-$267.0M).

gr4.evidence: Palo Alto Networks has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: GAAP results were losses as recently as FY2022, so it lacks the steady ten-year EPS record Graham requires, and FY2026 GAAP diluted EPS was only $0.40.

gr6.evidence: The share price is around 990 times trailing GAAP earnings, far above 15.

gr7.evidence: With a trailing P/E near 990 and price/book around 12 ($325B market cap vs $27,492M equity), the product is far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its firewalls and AI-driven SOC are among the best, but competitors offer comparable products, so it is not ten times better than the next best.

timing.evidence: Rising AI-enabled attacks and enterprise AI adoption are driving demand for security platforms just as it launches AI security products (Prisma AIRS) and consolidates vendors.

th3.evidence: It began by leading the then-new next-generation firewall niche after its 2005 founding and has expanded into SASE, SOC, cloud, identity and AI security.

team.evidence: CEO Nikesh Arora (since 2018) has led revenue from $3,408.4M in FY2020 to $11,480M in FY2026, with founder Nir Zuk still serving as CTO.

th5.evidence: It has a large direct sales force plus more than 8,700 channel partners worldwide.

durable.evidence: Deeply embedded security infrastructure is likely to last, but security technology shifts quickly (cloud, AI agents) and Microsoft, CrowdStrike and Zscaler are strong challengers.

th7.evidence: Its bet on 'platformization', consolidating many security tools into one vendor, was contrarian when announced in 2024, but rivals now pursue similar strategies.

trend.evidence: It is a leading beneficiary of cloud migration and AI adoption, with NGS ARR up 63% to $9.10B in Q4 FY2026.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth accelerated to 34% in Q4 FY2026 (helped by acquisitions) and analysts raised targets (e.g., Wells Fargo to $420, Citi to $432), but FY2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance implies only about 9% growth.

dr2.evidence: Cross-selling CyberArk identity and AI security could lift results, but integration costs and amortization also weigh on reported margins.

dr4.evidence: Security spending is resilient to the economic cycle, but a stock at about 90 times forward earnings is sensitive to interest rates.

dr6.evidence: Identifiable catalysts include CyberArk cross-sell, Prisma AIRS adoption and continued NGS ARR growth reported each quarter.

dr7.evidence: The business quality supports conviction, but valuation and acquisition risk argue against an outsized concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 70.4% in FY2026 (73.4% in FY2025), high though below Fortinet's 80.5% in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $4,113M against about $325B market cap is a yield of roughly 1.3%.

gb2.evidence: GAAP operating income of $695M is about 0.2% of an enterprise value near $319B.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback: revenue grew 24.5% in FY2026 and the stock is near record highs.

pa4.evidence: The business is unlikely to fail, but at about 90 times forward earnings a de-rating could cause large, lasting losses for buyers at today's price.

wo1.evidence: It is a leader in security for AI (Prisma AIRS, AI agent security via Koi and Portkey) and AI-driven SOC (XSIAM), but is not an AI platform builder itself.

wo2.evidence: There is no evidence of rapidly falling unit costs opening new demand; it sells premium-priced software and hardware.

wo3.evidence: It combines cloud computing and AI in its security products, but not other ARK platforms such as robotics or energy storage.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market is growing, but cybersecurity is unlikely to become many times larger within five years.

ac3.evidence: As a software-heavy security vendor (80% of FY2026 revenue from subscriptions and support), it is largely insulated from commodity prices.

ns1.evidence: Platform bundles and free transition periods pass some value to customers, but it remains a premium-priced vendor.

ns4.evidence: Its broader platform after CyberArk and Chronosphere could strengthen its position, but execution and competition make this uncertain.

va2.evidence: It addresses cyberattacks, a large, costly and growing problem for every organisation.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the AI and cloud security trend, but its roots are in firewalls and much of its AI capability was added through acquisitions (Koi, Portkey, Console).

tn2.evidence: Many still see it as a firewall vendor, while it is becoming an AI-era security platform across identity, observability and SOC, though the market already partly prices this in.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US software company with recurring revenue, outside all the zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year to $11,480M in FY2026, it was GAAP profitable ($307M), and cash plus investments of $7,906M exceed $1,774M of debt.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive ($4,113M in FY2026) and it had no debt before the CyberArk notes, with cash and short-term investments of $3,071M above $1,774M of debt at July 31, 2026.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 24.5% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 35.8% gives about 60.

tn8.evidence: Operating expenses rose about 34% (gross profit minus operating income, $7,382M vs $5,527M) while revenue grew 24.5% in FY2026.

tn9.evidence: It hits an instant kill: FY2026 GAAP operating margin was 6.1%, below 20%.

tn10.evidence: No major regulatory or legal threat is known beyond normal product-vulnerability and acquisition-review risks.

tn11.evidence: It provides an integrated cybersecurity platform that helps enterprises and governments stop cyberattacks, and charges mainly through subscriptions and support contracts plus firewall hardware sales.

tn13.evidence: Total 90: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth 10, operating margin 0, short interest 10 (2.6%), institutional ownership 10 (88%), revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return 10, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 10, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year, but operating margin fell from 13.5% in FY2025 to 6.1% in FY2026 after the CyberArk acquisition.

tn15.evidence: Liabilities ($20,968M) are under 4 times equity, but the current ratio is 0.87 ($8,643M / $9,923M) and assets excluding goodwill ($26,450M) are only about 1.3 times liabilities.

tn18.evidence: Nikesh Arora has a strong growth record since 2018, but he is not the founder, has under ten years in the role and has not been buying shares in the open market.

tn20.evidence: It has regularly beaten estimates, e.g., Q3 FY2026 revenue of $3.0B versus $2.94B expected and EPS of $0.85 versus $0.80.

tn21.evidence: It shows an acquisition spree (CyberArk, Chronosphere, Koi, Portkey, Console, Embrace in about a year), a falling GAAP operating margin and net insider selling while the stock runs.

tn22.evidence: It has $11,480M of revenue, $4,113M of free cash flow and does not sell shares to raise cash.

tn24.evidence: A free-cash-flow yield near 1.3% implies many years of growth well above the current ~24% (largely acquisition-boosted) rate.

tn25.evidence: Five years of FCF at a ~36% margin with 20%+ trimmed growth and 4% terminal growth at a 12% discount rate gives a value far below the ~$375-$397 share price.

tn26.evidence: It passes the Rule of 40 (about 60), but forward P/E near 90 against about 9% EPS growth gives a PEG near 10, well above 1.
